title: Mechanic
wiki_lead:
A mechanic is a skilled tradesperson who uses tools, procedures, and experiential knowledge to build, alter, maintain, repair, restore, test, or improve the capabilities of machinery, especially vehicles or other mechanical devices. The term previously referred to anyone in various handicraft trades, but it has referred specifically to those who work with machinery since the early 20th century. A technician is generally a mechanic who, through higher education, experience, or a non-proficiency-based title, engages in performance or instruction of more nuanced, technically challenging operations, and generally has a greater understanding of a system's operations and specifications.
Mechanics work across a wide range of disciplines, including automotive, energy, maritime, aeronautical, civil, domestic, mining, military, industrial, agricultural, and pharmaceutical. The responsibilities typically include inspecting equipment, diagnosing faults, setting parameters of moving assemblies, adjusting flow and pressures of fluid systems, verifying proper installation of new components if installed by secondary entities, and repairing or replacing components. They perform preventive maintenance to ensure machinery operates safely and efficiently. The profession developed rapidly during the Industrial Revolution, when increasing mechanisation created demand for specialised technical skills.
Training generally involves practical experience and apprenticeship, although vocational education, formal qualifications, and professional certification have become requirements in many fields. The modern mechanic works increasingly with electrical systems, computerised diagnostics, and advanced maintenance techniques, but generally will not directly work to fix problems associated with electronic, digital, or high-precision applications, as these specialties are pursued by electricians, computer scientists, and machinists. The occupation involves workplace hazards, including exposure to noise and chemicals, the danger of moving machinery, and risk of physical strain. It may involve working with, or to written instruction from: engineers, OEMs, customers, federal or state requirements, architects, designers, planners, testers, inspectors, or any body that may have authority or jurisdiction over the mechanic's task.

Etymology
The word mechanic is derived from Middle French mécanique, originating from Latin mechanicus, borrowed from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós; 'of machines, mechanical'), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ; 'machine, device') with the suffix -ικός (-ikós; 'relating to'). 
The word appeared in the Middle English poem Confessio Amantis, by John Gower, written in the late 14th century, spelt originally as mechanique, with the connotation of artisanry (a translation of the Latin term ars mechanica). During the 16th and 17th centuries, mechanic began to describe a labourer, and by pejoration, someone or something rude, common, vulgar. The word appears in Thomas Blount's 1656 dictionary Glossographia, providing the first definition for the occupation as "a Handicrafts man, a man of Occupation, a Trades-man".
The term previously referred to anyone in various handicraft trades, but it has referred specifically to those who work with machinery since the early 20th century.


Specialties

A mechanic is trained to inspect, maintain, and repair machinery to ensure optimal safety and performance, which may include interpreting and applying technical documentation, installing machinery, repairing or replacing components including consumables such as oils and filters, testing and diagnosing defects or issues, and certifying the machinery as fit for use. 
Mechanics carry out scheduled and chronicled preventive maintenance to maximize the lifespan of machinery.
Although there are general mechanics, most mechanics are formally-taught specialists of a particular type, such as aircraft, automotive, diesel, motorsport, bicycle, heavy equipment, industrial, marine, or heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC). Mechanics can work on-site or be mobile.
Modern work often involves electronic controls and computer-based diagnostic tools such as OBD testers or PC-based diagnostic systems.


Qualifications

Beginning in the early 20th century, the process of becoming a mechanic was formalised, and standard skill building courses introduced. 
In many jurisdictions formal certification of a mechanic's skill in their field is required before they are permitted to carry out work. For example, an automotive mechanic in Western Australia must hold a "motor vehicle repairer's certificate" (or work under the supervision of a mechanic with that certification) to offer services to the public.
Many mechanics in developing countries and even in developed ones often learn through apprenticeship. 


Types


Aircraft maintenance technician

An aircraft maintenance technician (also known as aviation mechanic) specialises in repairing and maintaining aircraft, including planes and helicopters. They work on engines, landing gear, avionics, computerized systems, and other mechanical/electrical systems. 
Typically, the profession is managed by a national regulator, such as the Federal Aviation Administration, European Union Aviation Safety Agency, or Transport Canada. Obtaining a license requires passing exams on the related laws and aircraft systems, apprenticeship hours, and, in some countries, the completion of specific maintenance tasks signed off by a licensed mechanic.
Aircraft licenses may have a sub-category or specialisation, such as Canada's AME-M, AME-S, and AME-E licenses covering general maintenance, structures, and avionics, respectively.
Aircraft differ from most other vehicles in the number of inspections they require at specified calendar or flight hours. Line maintenance refers to the inspections and tasks handled between flights at an airport, including minor issues reported by the pilot or flight crew. Base and heavy maintenance refer to intensive inspections and overhauls handled at specialised hangars that involve a larger crew. Inspections are outlined by the manufacturer in a Maintenance Planning Document, while tasks are outlined in the Aircraft Maintenance Manual. Often, a critical safety issue will require an Airworthiness Directive, similar to a recall in automotive vehicles, in which all aircraft operators complete certain maintenance tasks to keep the aircraft airworthy. The most notable example is AD 2020-25844 following the grounding of the Boeing 737 MAX.


Auto mechanic

An auto mechanic repairs and maintains automobiles. They perform standard maintenance while inspecting vehicles for damage and wear. They test components using diagnostic equipment to replace wear-down or defective parts, and perform routine service such as oil changes or brake work. Other responsibilities include troubleshooting and fixing hydraulic lines, and repairing electric systems. 
As of 1 October 2026, the median pay for an auto mechanic is around $54,959 per year.
Motorsport teams employ specialized automotive mechanics to work on race cars. Historically, some motorsport series featured riding mechanics. As the maintenance performed by a pit crew is done during the race itself, the mechanics involved are specially trained for minimal time loss with each pit stop.


Diesel mechanic

A diesel mechanic specialises in the inspection, maintenance, and repair of diesel-powered road vehicles, such as buses, tractor units, box trucks, dump trucks, garbage trucks. They also work on heavy construction and farm machinery, including excavators, backhoes, combine harvesters, and tractors. 
The median pay for a diesel mechanic in the United States is around $65,000 per year.


Bicycle mechanic

A bicycle mechanic specialises in repairing, adjusting, maintaining, and replacing parts of a bicycle. They work on frames, wheels, brakes, gears, and other mechanical or electronic components.


Industrial mechanic

An industrial mechanic works in industrial settings such as factories, manufacturing plants, and production plants. Industrial mechanics are responsible for the maintenance and repair of equipment such as machine tools, pumps, generators, and other heavy equipment. They identify mechanical problems, repair or replace damaged components, and adjust equipment to maintain proper operation. They also perform routine maintenance, such as cleaning and lubricating machinery, and use technical manuals and diagnostic equipment to locate faults. Some industrial mechanics use computerized diagnostic systems and vibration analysis to identify problems with machinery.


Marine mechanic
A marine mechanic specialises in repairing and maintaining watercraft. They work on Outboard Motor, propellers, steering systems, and other mechanical components of boats. In Britain, the ship repair and maintenance industry reached its peak in the 1940s, when over 20,000 men and women were employed for such work in Merseyside. Specialities include fitters in the engine room, boilermakers, blacksmiths, plumbers, riveters, burners, and welders.


Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning mechanic
A HVAC mechanic (heating, ventilation, and air conditioning mechanic) specialises in the maintenance, inspection, repair and installation of HVAC and refrigeration systems. These include furnaces, air-conditioning systems, heat pumps, ventilation systems and refrigeration units. In the US the career is expected to grow by 11% between 2025 and 2035. The median annual wage for HVAC mechanics in the US was $61,010 in May 2025. 


Line mechanic
A line mechanic specialises in ensuring proper operation of different kinds of machinery and equipment. Their main focus is maintenance and repair; playing an important role in keeping production lines effective and efficient. The occupation is expected to grow strongly through 2035, because of factors like grid modernisation, clean energy transmission and increasing retirement rates. As of October 2026 their median income the United States was $60,039.


Occupational hazards

Mechanics may face a variety of occupational hazards. They are frequently exposed to elevated sound levels; in an analysis of 1999–2004 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data, vehicle and mobile equipment mechanics and repairers employed in manufacturing had an 82% prevalence of hazardous workplace noise exposure, the highest among occupations in that sector.
Mechanics are also frequently exposed to harmful chemicals. Exposure to engine oils causes contact dermatitis to be over twice as prevalent among automotive mechanics as office workers. Automotive mechanics are exposed to elevated levels of volatile organic compounds when applying brake cleaner and painting. 
These chemicals increase the prevalence of respiratory health conditions and impair lung function. Mechanics are also at risk of carbon monoxide poisoning, with a study by the United States National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health reporting 34 fatalities caused by vehicle exhaust from 1992–2008. 
Aircraft mechanics are exposed to jet fuel, which epidemiological research indicates may increase the risk of cancer or neurological, respiratory, and cognitive problems.
Poor ergonomics also contributes to workplace injuries. Mechanics can experience repetitive strain injuries and pain caused by lifting heavy objects or maintaining awkward postures to reach inside machinery. Vibrations produced by power tools put mechanics at risk of nerve damage, which can lead to Raynaud syndrome, neurosensory injury, and carpal tunnel syndrome. Musculoskeletal disorders associated with mechanic work are most prevalent in the lower back, shoulders, and wrists.

grok_lead: A mechanic is a skilled tradesperson who diagnoses, repairs, and maintains mechanical equipment, such as engines, vehicles, and industrial machinery. Mechanics typically work in automotive repair shops, factories, or service centers, using specialized tools and diagnostic software to identify issues and perform fixes ranging from routine maintenance like oil changes to complex overhauls of transmissions or electrical systems. The profession demands physical stamina, as workers often lift heavy parts, work in noisy or greasy environments, and may face high rates of on-the-job injuries compared to other occupations. Mechanics specialize in various areas, including automotive service for cars and light trucks, diesel technicians for heavy vehicles, heavy equipment technicians for construction and agricultural machinery, and industrial mechanics for factory equipment. Entry into the field usually requires a high school diploma followed by postsecondary training, such as a certificate or associate degree in automotive technology, though some gain skills through apprenticeships or on-the-job experience. Certifications from organizations like the National Institute for Automotive Service Excellence (ASE) enhance employability and are often required for tasks involving refrigerants or advanced diagnostics. In the United States, as of May 2024, the median annual wage for automotive service technicians and mechanics was $49,670, with employment projected to grow 4% from 2024 to 2034, about as fast as the average for all occupations, due to more vehicles on the road and the need to maintain complex safety features, although the rise of electric vehicles may limit some demand.
